narrative.overview: rack.bar looks like a precision instrument that lives on the competition platform. The venue supplies the world: black rubber underfoot, chrome sleeve under arena light, and the only real color in the room is the plates themselves. The instrument supplies the character: engineered, glanceable, chalk-proof -- monospaced numerals that never jitter, one yellow that means "act here," and controls big enough to hit between sets with taped thumbs. The voice is sharp, physical, gym-native. The anti-reference is the generic calculator app: no gradient-happy dashboards, no floating cards, no colors that mean nothing. Every hue on screen is either the near-monochrome chrome of the instrument or the domain-true color of a plate a lifter would name out loud ("throw a red on").
keyCharacteristics: Near-black tonal surfaces; saturated color is reserved for plates and the single accent.
Monospaced, tabular numerals everywhere a weight is displayed.
Pill geometry for controls; discs and sheets are the only large shapes.
Flat at rest; shadow means a physically real thing (a disc's rim, an overlay hovering above the app).
One accent (Plate Yellow) marking the active segment and the primary action.

rules.name: The Plates Own the Color Rule
rules.body: UI chrome stays near-monochrome; saturated color belongs to the plates and to the one accent that borrows a plate's hex. Never introduce a new saturated color for interface purposes.

rules.name: The Domain Color Rule
rules.body: Plate hexes are physical facts (CONTEXT.md). Color is never the sole channel: a numeral or shape always disambiguates alongside it.

rules.name: The Tabular Digits Rule
rules.body: Every weight readout uses tabular/monospaced numerals (tnum or the mono face) so digits never jitter as values change.

rules.name: The Engraved Numeral Rule
rules.body: A disc's weight is stamped on it: rotated -90 degrees, JetBrains Mono 800, ink chosen for contrast against the plate color (dark on white/yellow, white otherwise).

rules.name: The Physical Lift Rule
rules.body: Shadow means physicality, never decoration: a disc has a rim because a plate does; a sheet casts a shadow because it hovers above the app. Nothing else gets one.

dos: Do style every surface through --rack-* tokens in tokens.css -- one source of truth per value (ADR-0001); reach for the precise named tier (e.g. --rack-border-strong), never the legacy collapsed aliases (--rack-bg, --rack-muted, --rack-line) in new code.
Do use the shared DISC_FILL gradient + disc shadow for any plate-colored surface, with per-color ink (dark on white/yellow, white otherwise).
Do pair every color-coded element with a numeral or shape cue -- color is never the sole channel.
Do keep touch targets at 44px minimum with the press-scale feedback; chalk-hands usability is a product commitment.
Do use tabular/mono numerals for every weight readout, rolling on change (numRoll .26s).
donts: Don't introduce new saturated interface colors; the plates own the color (accent yellow is the 15 kg plate's hex, danger the 25 kg red).
Don't restyle, lighten, or "theme" the plate palette -- the hexes are domain facts lifters navigate by.
Don't add shadows to resting UI; depth at rest is tonal (the surface ladder). Shadow is reserved for discs and overlays (the Physical Lift Rule).
Don't gradient the share card's chips -- flat fill + inset ring is the spec'd, deliberate exception.
Don't add a scrim behind the keypad or an outside-tap dismissal -- its scrimless brightness is a deliberate fidelity call so the bar stays live while typing.
Don't diverge from the design handoff's look (docs/design-handoff/) in build slices; aesthetic changes route through a design pass.
